REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript presents a novel and well-constructed strategy for the targeted treatment of
AIDs by engineering CD4mAb-BMSCs combined with a liposomal delivery system carrying
RORγt inverse agonists. The study is conceptually innovative and supported by
comprehensive in vitro and in vivo data, including two disease models (PO and RA). The dual
approach—integrating targeted cell therapy and controlled drug release—offers strong
potential for translational application. However, several key issues require clarification and
additional discussion before the manuscript can be considered for publication. These include
mechanistic insights into selective targeting, the rationale for specific experimental choices,
and aspects related to clinical safety and translatability. I provide specific comments below to
help the authors further improve the clarity, completeness, and impact of their work.
Introduction
1. It would be helpful for readers if the authors could elaborate on the underlying mechanism
by which antibody conjugation to the cell surface prevents non-specific cellular
internalization. Clarifying this point in the manuscript would greatly aid in understanding how
selective delivery to Th17 cells is achieved.
Response:
Thank you for your valuable suggestion. Unlike ADCs, which require target antigens (Ag) to
undergo receptor-mediated endocytosis for efficient payload delivery (Fig. 1a), Ac-MSCs
transport their internalized payload to inflammation sites, where it is extracellularly released
and diffuses into adjacent target cells (Fig. 1b). Therefore, our system does not ensure that
Cdg enters only Th17 cells but rather promotes the local enrichment of Cdg around CD4⁺ T
cells at inflamed sites. Since Th17 cells predominate among CD4⁺ T cells in inflamed tissues,
increasing the local concentration of Cdg in their vicinity facilitates its action on Th17 cells.
This mechanism eliminates the need for antigen internalization, allowing Ac-MSCs to target a
wide range of surface proteins and achieve site-specific drug accumulation rather than cell-
restricted delivery.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised introduction (Page 3, line 73-78).
2. Have the authors considered potential off-target effects when CD4mAb-BMSCs bind to
naïve CD4⁺ T cells rather than Th17 cells? Any possible immunological side effects arising
from non-specific targeting should be discussed.
Response:
Thank you for your comment. Although CD4 is broadly expressed among helper T-cell
subsets, our in vivo data indicates that AcM-DDS preferentially accumulates in inflamed
tissues enriched with activated CD4⁺ T cells (Fig. 2g and 2h), where Th17 cells predominate
(Supplementary Fig. 1). As naïve CD4⁺ T cells are relatively limited in inflamed sites, their
potential engagement by AcM-DDS is expected to be limited. Consistent with this, no
apparent immunological side effects or abnormal immune activation were observed in either
the RA or PO models following repeated administration. Moreover, since MSCs are
inherently immunomodulatory and non-cytotoxic, transient interactions with non-activated
CD4⁺ T cells are unlikely to cause adverse immune responses.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised discussion (Page 25, line 478-
485).
3. Could the authors explain why liposomes were chosen as the delivery vehicle for the
RORγt inverse agonists? It would be helpful to understand whether liposomes offer any
particular advantages over other nanoparticle systems in this context.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. Liposomes were chosen as the delivery
vehicle for the RORγt inverse agonists mainly due to their favorable structural features, high
drug-loading capacity, and well-established clinical safety profile.
Structurally, liposomes possess a phospholipid bilayer architecture that closely resembles
biological membranes, which not only enhances biocompatibility but also facilitates efficient
cellular uptake and intracellular drug release. In addition, their amphiphilic nature enables the
efficient encapsulation of both hydrophilic and hydrophobic drugs; in this study, the
hydrophobic RORγt inverse agonists were effectively incorporated into the lipid bilayer,
achieving a high drug-loading efficiency and good stability.
Importantly, liposomes are one of the few nanoscale delivery systems that have been
extensively validated in clinical settings, with several FDA-approved formulations (e.g.,
Doxil, AmBisome), demonstrating excellent safety and translational potential. These
advantages collectively make liposomes a rational and reliable choice for constructing the
AcM-DDS platform in our study.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised introduction (Page 4, line 99-102).
Results
1. Figure 3f, Supplementary Figure 4a: The authors suggest that glycoprotein azidation of the
cell membrane may influence small molecule efflux. Please provide a more detailed
mechanistic explanation and supporting evidence to substantiate this claim.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and apologize for any lack of
clarity in our original manuscript that may have led to this misunderstanding. In fact, we had
performed additional experiments to further investigate whether metabolic glycan labeling
and subsequent azidation affect small-molecule efflux. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 4b,
further investigation using the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) inhibitor verapamil revealed that N3-
mBMSCs exhibited an efflux capacity comparable to that of verapamil-treated mBMSCs,
suggesting that glycoprotein azidation does not markedly impair membrane transporter
function.
We acknowledge, however, that this validation remains preliminary. Due to the peripheral
nature of this observation relative to the central focus of our study, we were unable to pursue
more extensive mechanistic experiments at this stage. Nevertheless, we are currently
performing transcriptomic analyses of mBMSCs, CD4-mBMSCs, CdgLipo-mBMSCs, and
AcM-DDS cells, which may provide additional insight into potential changes in membrane
transport–related pathways (NEW supplemented Fig. 5a-5f). We plan to further explore this
mechanism in future studies.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 10, line 224-231).
2. Figure 3h, Could the authors clarify why osteogenic differentiation was evaluated rather
than adipogenic or chondrogenic differentiation? For applications in arthritis models,
chondrogenic potential would appear more directly relevant. Additionally, the increased
proliferation observed in AcM-DDS compared to mBMSCs warrants further explanation.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important comment and apologize for the oversight
in our initial submission. In the revised version, we have now added these results:
chondrogenic differentiation was evaluated by Alcian Blue staining (NEW Fig. 3h) and
adipogenic differentiation by Oil Red O staining (NEW Fig. 3i), showing comparable
differentiation potential among the different groups.
Regarding the increased proliferation of AcM-DDS compared to mBMSCs, this is consistent
with our transcriptomic analysis, which revealed upregulated expression of proliferation-
related genes such as Fgf2 and Ptgs2 (NEW Supplementary Fig. 5f).
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 10, line 220-223).
3. Figure 6f, The use of Safranin O staining might provide clearer visualization of cartilage
morphology and thickness compared to Toluidine Blue. The authors may consider discussing
this alternative method.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In the initial submission, we had
repeatedly attempted Safranin O/Fast Green staining on paraffin-embedded knee joint
sections; however, the staining results were unstable and unsatisfactory, likely due to pH
values in the decalcifying solution, as reported in the literature (Hayer et al., 2021). Because
the available knee sections were exhausted during these attempts, we adopted toluidine
blue—a more stable alternative under our conditions—for the initial histological assessment.
During the revision stage, we carefully re-collected the preserved ankle joints, initiated a new
decalcification process, and successfully performed Safranin O/Fast Green staining. The new
results are presented in Figure 6h-i. Moreover, H&E staining of the corresponding ankle
joints has been added and integrated with the knee joint histology (previously shown in Fig.
6e) in the NEW Supplementary Figure 13e.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 21, line 411-418).
4. Figure 7a–c, Supplementary Figure 9: Articular cartilage consists solely of chondrocytes.
Therefore, the DAB signals observed within the cartilage layers are more likely to represent
gene expression in chondrocytes rather than infiltrating immune cells. Since immune cells
such as T cells typically reside in the synovium or synovial fluid, analysis of these regions
may be more appropriate for confirming T cell localization.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. Since RA is primarily driven by
synovial inflammation, we agree that the synovium is the more relevant tissue for analyzing T
cell localization. In the revised manuscript, while maintaining the original data, we have re-
focused the magnified images to specifically highlight the synovium, meniscus, and cartilage
regions. These modifications can be found in Figure 7a-d and Supplementary Figure 14a-b,
allowing for a more accurate representation of T cell distribution within the relevant tissues.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 22, line 425-433).
Discussion
1. The Discussion section largely reiterates content from the Introduction and Results. It
would be more impactful if this section focused on interpretation and implications of the
findings. For instance, potential mechanisms that enable selective drug delivery to Th17 cells
without unintended release could be discussed.
Response:
Thank you for your suggestion. The AcM-DDS system was designed to enrich the local
concentration of Cedirogant around CD4⁺ T cells rather than to achieve cell-internal release as
in ADC therapeutics. In vitro release assays showed that approximately 25% of the payload
was released within 24 h, indicating that limited diffusion occurs before complete tissue
homing. Therefore, we acknowledge that unintended partial release cannot be entirely
excluded. A major direction for future optimization is to ensure that nanoparticles are released
from MSC carriers only after tissue homing. To reduce premature drug release from
intracellularly loaded MSCs and to ensure release only after homing, several complementary
strategies are feasible. The possible strategies include inducible CRISPRi/siRNA to reversibly
downregulate ABC transporters, or engineering MSCs to undergo inflammation-triggered
exocytosis.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Discussion (Page 25, line 514-
526).
2. The authors suggest that cell-mediated delivery could help overcome the clinical safety
issues previously associated with Cedirogant. If so, it is necessary to clearly explain how
AcM-DDS addresses these safety concerns. Moreover, supporting data regarding the safety of
this delivery system should be included to substantiate this claim.
Response:
Thank you for valuable comment. Cedirogant previously showed unfavorable systemic
exposure and metabolic instability in preclinical studies, including body weight loss and
gastrointestinal toxicity observed in a 39-week dog study (Tyring et al., 2024). In our
experiments, the treatment durations were considerably shorter (1 week for the PO model and
5 weeks for the RA model). Histological analysis of the small intestine and colon revealed no
apparent injury in either the Cdg-alone or AcM-DDS groups. These findings suggest that, in
our models, AcM-DDS primarily enhances local Cedirogant efficacy at inflammatory sites
rather than reducing gastrointestinal side effects.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Discussion (Page 25, line 501-
506).
In response to the reviewer’s concern regarding the systemic safety of our AcM-DDS system,
we have now included additional biochemical analyses of hepatic and renal function in RA
mice (Supplementary Fig. 15a). The results showed that serum levels of ALT, AST, BUN, and
creatinine remained within the normal physiological range across all treatment groups, with
no significant differences compared to the control group. These findings further confirm that
repeated administration of AcM-DDS does not induce hepatotoxicity or nephrotoxicity,
thereby strengthening the overall safety profile of our delivery system.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 22, line 448-451).
3. Systemically administered mBMSCs may accumulate in major organs such as the liver,
lungs, and spleen, raising potential safety concerns including tumorigenicity. In addition,
when translating to human applications, issues such as the immunogenicity of CD4 antibodies
and Cedirogant, dosing, and scalability should be considered. Discussion of these factors
would enhance the clinical relevance and translational potential of the study.
Response:
As mentioned in our previous response, we have supplemented the manuscript with
Supplementary Fig. 15a, which presents additional biochemical analyses of hepatic and renal
function in RA mice. The serum levels of ALT, AST, BUN, and creatinine in all treatment
groups remained within normal physiological ranges, showing no significant differences
compared with the control group. These data further substantiate the systemic safety of our
AcM-DDS platform and demonstrate that repeated administration does not cause detectable
hepatic or renal toxicity. (Page 22, line 448-451)
The overall safety profile of AcM-DDS depends primarily on two components: the
biodistribution of the carrier BMSCs and the localization of the encapsulated small-molecule
drug. AcM-DDS functions by promoting BMSC accumulation at inflammatory sites and
consequently enriching the local concentration of Cdg in these regions. Therefore, at an
equivalent systemic dose, the potential systemic toxicity of AcM-DDS should not exceed that
of either BMSCs or Cdg administered alone. Notably, the localized enrichment at inflamed
tissues may produce higher local drug concentrations, which could enhance efficacy but also
requires dose optimization to avoid local adverse effects. In our current dosing regimen, no
tissue damage or inflammatory exacerbation was observed at the injection or inflammatory
sites.
Binding of the CD4 antibody to the CD4 receptor on T cells represents another potential
source of immunological concern, as it could interfere with endogenous ligand interactions
such as CXCL12 binding. However, it is worth noting that CD4-targeting monoclonal
antibodies have already been approved for clinical use and exhibit favorable safety profiles.
The CD4 antibody selected in this study, therefore, offers a relatively safer targeting option
compared to unvalidated antigens. Together, these findings support the safety and
translational feasibility of AcM-DDS, although further optimization of dosing and long-term
evaluation will be required for future clinical application.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Discussion (Page 26, line 539-
543).
Additional Comments
1. The manuscript would benefit from a discussion on the in vivo retention time of AcM-DDS
and the duration of its anti-inflammatory effects. If relevant experiments have been
conducted, presenting this data would strengthen the translational significance of the work.
Response:
Thank you for your careful review and insightful comments. Bioluminescence tracking
revealed that AcM-DDS persisted at inflammatory sites for up to 96 hours post-injection (Fig
2g), correlating with sustained IL-17A suppression. The extended retention underscores its
potential for enhanced anti-inflammatory efficacy. Although real-time expression of IL-17A
or other inflammatory cytokines were not continuously monitored, endpoint analyses
demonstrated that AcM-DDS treatment achieved the greatest reduction in IL-17A, IL-21, IL-
22, and other proinflammatory cytokines compared with all control groups. As shown in Fig.
2g and 2h, CD4-mBMSCs exhibited longer retention at inflamed tissues than unmodified
BMSCs. Furthermore, in the cytokine profiling assays, CD4-mBMSCs showed stronger
suppression of G-CSF and IL-12p40 than mBMSCs (Fig 5e), suggesting that even in the
absence of CDG loading, enhanced localization and prolonged residence of MSCs at inflamed
sites contribute significantly to their anti-inflammatory activity.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 16, line 331-334).
2. The immunomodulatory effects of BMSCs and the pharmacological effects of Cedirogant
are not clearly delineated. Without appropriate experimental controls (e.g., CD4mAb-BMSCs
+ empty liposomes, or repeated dosing of CdgLipo alone), it is difficult to assess their relative
contributions. Additional discussion or clarification of this limitation would improve the
mechanistic understanding of the system.
Response:
Thank you for your comments. The immunomodulatory functions of BMSCs are well
established and include suppression of T-cell activation, promotion of Treg differentiation,
inhibition of proinflammatory cytokine release, and secretion of trophic factors that support
tissue repair. These properties contribute to the therapeutic effects observed in both the PO
and RA models, where BMSCs alone attenuated inflammation and improved tissue
morphology.
Cedirogant, a potent RORγt inverse agonist, acts primarily by downregulating Th17 activity
and IL-17A–driven cytokine signaling. In both PO and RA models, Th17-derived cytokines
(IL-17A, IL-21, and IL-22) are important mediators of immune-driven pathology. However,
in the RA model, CdgLipo alone provided limited bone-protective benefit, as shown in Fig.
6b–i, despite comparable suppression of IL-17A⁺CD4⁺ T cells (11.4% in the Cdg group vs.
11.5% in the CD4-mBMSC group, Fig. 7i).
When combined within the AcM-DDS system, the dual actions of BMSC-mediated
immunomodulation and Cedirogant-mediated Th17 inhibition produced a clear synergistic
effect. AcM-DDS treatment exhibited superior anti-inflammatory and bone-protective
outcomes compared with either BMSC or Cedirogant monotherapy, including CD4-mBMSC.
These findings suggest that Th17 suppression contributes to therapeutic efficacy of BMSCs to
promote tissue protection and repair. The detailed mechanisms underlying this synergy
warrant further investigation.
3. While AcM-DDS is reported to suppress Th17 cells primarily through IL-17A inhibition,
Th17 cells also secrete other proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-21, IL-22, and GM-CSF.
Inclusion or discussion of these additional markers would help define the extent of Th17
modulation more comprehensively.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We completely agree that Th17 cells
secrete multiple proinflammatory cytokines beyond IL-17A, including IL-21, IL-22, and GM-
CSF, which together contribute to Th17-driven immune responses. In the revised manuscript,
we have expanded our analysis to include these cytokines. Specifically, immunofluorescence
staining demonstrated that AcM-DDS markedly reduced IL-21 (NEW Fig. 5a-b) and IL-22
(NEW Fig. 5c-d) expression in dorsal skin tissues, while Luminex multiplex assay confirmed
a significant suppression of GM-CSF (NEW Fig. 5g). These results further substantiate that
AcM-DDS exerts a broad inhibitory effect on Th17-associated cytokine production rather
than acting solely through IL-17A suppression.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 16, line 315-320).

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This study demonstrated the construction of a “live drug carrier”, proposed to be CD-4 tagged
BM-MSCs, loaded with Cdg encapsulating liposomes for application in autoimmune diseases
like psoriasis and arthritis. However the current study has certain gaps which need to be
addressed before it can be considered suitable for publication.
1. As per the authors, MSCs act as live drug carriers and will release the drug in inflammatory
milieu without the need for internalization. However, the authors may clarify that if MSCs
burst to release the drug in the inflammatory milieu, it will also be released in the circulation,
what effect that may have? Authors may evaluate the same in the mice blood as well.
Response:
Thank you for raising this important point. We fully acknowledge the concern regarding the
potential release of the drug into circulation if MSCs were to burst in the inflammatory
milieu.
In our study, we did consider evaluating the effects of drug release in circulation. However,
due to the low drug loading in the MSCs, we encountered significant technical challenges in
quantifying the drug concentration in the blood and local tissues of mice. Despite our efforts,
including attempts to use LC-MS for drug concentration measurements, the sensitivity and
detection limits of the current analytical techniques were not sufficient to reliably measure the
drug levels in circulation or tissues at these low concentrations.
We have discussed these technical limitations in the manuscript and acknowledge that more

2. The specificity of the graphical abstract with respect to the article maybe improved.
Currently, the abstract does not represent the article, but seems like a generalized poster.
Specifically, there is no specific mention of the RORγT antagonist, and it is not evident from
the graphical abstract that the study was performed in psoriasis and arthritis models. The
layout and content need to be improved.
Response:
Thank you for the constructive feedback. We agree that the original graphical abstract lacked
specificity, so we have revised Figure 1 accordingly. Without changing the overall structure,
we now explicitly highlight the use of RORγt inverse agonists and clearly indicate the disease
contexts (psoriasis and arthritis) examined in this study. In addition, we added new panels d-e
as application examples: CD4mAb-conjugated BMSCs loaded with RORγt inverse agonists
demonstrate therapeutic efficacy in the IMQ-induced psoriasis-like (PO) model (panel d) and
the collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) model (panel e). We also refined the layout to improve
clarity and narrative flow. We believe these changes address the concerns regarding
specificity, disease models, and layout, and better align the graphical abstract with the
manuscript. We greatly appreciate your suggestion.
3. In Fig. 2 (d), the authors could have captured different frames and presented the
quantification of the results, apart from only the representative images to demonstrate the CD-
4+ T cells and CD4-BM-MSCs
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. In response, we have
performed quantification of the binding shown in the original Fig. 2d (now Fig.2e), as
requested. Specifically, N₃-mBMSCs and CD4-mBMSCs were co-cultured with CD4⁺ T cells,
and the ratio of CD4⁺ T cells bound per MSC was calculated across 10 randomly selected

Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In response, we quantified the
accumulation of MSCs in inflamed skin following intravenous administration. DiD-labeled
mBMSCs and CD4-mBMSCs were injected into IMQ-induced PO mice, and dorsal skin was
harvested 72 h post-injection for flow cytometric analysis. Consistent with the in vivo

mBMSCs.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 7, line 159-161).
5. In Fig. 2 (f), the authors suggest a significant difference in the skin and the spleen, however
the authors may re-check whether there is a significant difference in the liver group at 24h as
well.
Response:
Thank you for raising this important point. We carefully re-examined the raw data for the
liver at 24 h and performed repeated statistical analyses. Both an unpaired two-tailed t test
and a Tukey’s post hoc test (following two-way ANOVA) consistently indicated no
statistically significant difference for the liver at 24 h (p = 0.0589). These results are fully

6. As per the statement of the authors, Cedirogant was discontinued due to off-targeting and
safety issues. However, this does not seem in line with available literature and data about the

by the manufacturer due to some new unfavourable toxicology findings in preclinial studied,
Therefore, the authors may explain the plausibility of their hypothesis, strategizing to load
cedirogant for mitigating off-targeting.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive comment. Cedirogant (ABBV-157) was
discontinued due to preclinical toxicology findings related to GI track. In the 39-week dog
toxicity study, body weight loss and gastrointestinal toxicity were observed (Tyring et al.,
2024). The chronic suppression of Th17 cells could disrupt the delicate balance between Th17
cells and Tregs in the gut. Th17 cells are critical for maintaining intestinal homeostasis by
producing cytokines such as IL-17 and IL-22, which support epithelial barrier integrity,
antimicrobial peptide production, and mucosal defense (Ohara et al., 2024). This disruption
may impair mucosal immunity, reduce epithelial regeneration, and compromise barrier
function, leading to intestinal toxicity. In our short-term models (1-5 weeks), histological
analyses revealed no intestinal damage in either the CdgLipo or AcM-DDS groups (NEW
supplementary Fig 16). These findings suggest that, in our models, AcM-DDS primarily
enhances local Cdg efficacy at inflammatory sites rather than reducing gastrointestinal side
effects.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Discussion (Page 25, line 501-
508).

determined that the drug loading capacity of Cdg in liposomes was approximately 8.48%,
with an encapsulation efficiency of 92.8%” It is unclear whether 8,48% of Cdg was loaded
into liposomes and 92.8% lipososomes were able to take up the drug, or does it mean
something else.
Response:
We sincerely thank you for this valuable comment. We have revised the sentence to clarify the
meaning of both parameters. Specifically, the drug loading capacity (8.48%) refers to the
drug-to-lipid weight ratio, while the encapsulation efficiency (92.8%) represents the
proportion of total Cdg encapsulated within the liposomes. The revised text in the manuscript
now reads:
“HPLC analysis revealed that the liposomes had a drug loading capacity of approximately
8.48% (w/w, drug-to-lipid ratio) and an encapsulation efficiency of 92.8% (percentage of
total Cdg encapsulated in liposomes).” (Page 9, Line 185-187)
8. The authors may quantify how many CD-4 receptors are present per MSCS, and how many
drug loaded lipososmes are internalized per MSC, as this will be relevant to determine the
clinical applicability.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and instructive comment, which helped us
recognize the importance of quantitatively characterizing the surface modification and
cellular uptake efficiency of our system. In the revised manuscript, we have now provided
detailed quantitative data addressing both aspects.
“Quantitative fluorescence analysis indicated that when 25 µg of DBCO-CD4mAb-FITC
was conjugated with 1 × 10⁶ N₃-mBMSCs, approximately 2,500 antibody molecules were
anchored per cell on average.” (Page 6, Line 144-146)
“Furthermore, quantitative fluorescence analysis based on Cy5 intensity allowed
estimation of nanoparticle uptake per cell, indicating that each CD4-mBMSC internalized
approximately 1.15 × 10⁴ CdgLipo particles on average.” (Page 9, Line 201-204)
The corresponding experimental procedures for these quantifications have also been added to
the Methods section for clarity and reproducibility.
9. The authors could have included an only drug group (without liposomes encapsulation) to
demonstrate the off-targeting effect suggested by them. Additionally, a positive control, e.g.
a commercial treatment option could have been included.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we
have now added animal experiments in IMQ-induced PO mice to address this point (NEW
Supplementary Fig. 7a-i). Specifically, we included a free Cedirogant (Cdg) treatment group
to evaluate the effect of the drug without liposome encapsulation, as well as a positive control
group using methotrexate (MTX), which is widely used as a positive control in the IMQ-
induced PO model (Xie et al., 2018). Our results indicate that both free Cdg and MTX
produced modest therapeutic improvements, whereas repeated dosing of CdgLipo showed
slightly enhanced efficacy. Importantly, all these treatments were still less effective than
AcM-DDS, demonstrating the superior targeting and therapeutic advantage of our antibody-
guided, liposome-loaded MSC system. We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion,
which helped us strengthen the experimental validation and provide a clearer comparison with
conventional treatments.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 14, line 280-288).
10. It is unclear how the authors determined the dose of the treatment groups in animals. The
authors may test variable doses and present the data for the chosen dose.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the dosing details in our animal
experiments. For the MSC-based treatment groups, we administered 1 × 106 cells per mouse,
as this is the most commonly used dosage in preclinical studies of MSCs for autoimmune
diseases, providing a widely accepted reference for efficacy and safety (González et al.,
2009).
For Cedirogant (Cdg), each mouse received 4.5 mg/kg, which corresponds to the maximum
amount of drug that can be internalized by 1 × 106 MSCs. Importantly, there are currently no
published preclinical animal studies for Cdg, so we referred to human clinical trial data.
In Phase 1 studies (Maier et al., 2024), oral doses of Cdg ranged from 20–750 mg as a single
dose and 75–375 mg/day for multiple doses. Using the FDA’s Meeh-Rubner conversion
factor (Reagan-Shaw et al., 2008), this roughly corresponds to 15.4–77.1 mg/kg/day oral
dosing in mice. Considering the oral bioavailability in humans (Maier et al., 2024), the
equivalent intravenous dose in mice would be approximately 6 mg/kg. Our chosen dose of
4.5 mg/kg per 1 × 106 MSCs is therefore a conservative estimate, lower than the clinical-
equivalent dose.
Since this study is primarily a proof-of-concept, we did not explore a full range of high,
medium, and low doses. Future studies may optimize dosing to evaluate dose-dependency and
further refine therapeutic efficacy.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 13, line 262-266).
11. Time point based skin localization study in animal could have been included to determine
the highest localisation of drug at a given time point. This could have also given insights on
whether liposome is accelerating the time of delivery, as early relief might also be important
clinically.
Response:
Thank you for your valuable suggestion regarding the time-point based skin localization
study. In our current study, we performed in vivo imaging (IVIS) to monitor the distribution
of BMSCs and observed that the fluorescence signal peaked in the skin between 72- and 96-
hours post-injection, indicating the highest localization of BMSCs in the inflamed tissue (Fig.
2g). However, we understand that evaluating the drug concentration at these time points is
crucial for further insights.
We attempted to quantify the drug levels in skin tissue using LC-MS, but the results were not
successful. The primary challenge was that the amount of drug loaded into the MSCs was
relatively low, and consequently, the drug concentration in the tissues was below the detection
threshold of the LC-MS method. To overcome this limitation, we would need to increase the
drug load in the MSCs or use a larger animal model (e.g., rats), where the drug quantity in
tissues would be more detectable. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and will consider
these strategies in future studies to enable more accurate quantification of drug delivery over
time.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Discussion (Page 26, line 517-523).
12. The data in Fig 6 (d-f) may be quantified and evaluated for statistical significance
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have added
quantitative analysis for the data shown in originally Fig 6d-f. Specifically, for micro-CT
analysis (now Fig. 6c), we quantified the subchondral bone parameters, including BV/TV,
SMI, and Tb. N, and observed significant improvements in the mBMSCs-based treatment
groups (Fig. 6d-e, Supplementary Fig. 13b-c). Quantification of histological data (Fig. 6g, 6i,
Supplementary Fig. 13d-e) was also included, with statistical significance now evaluated for
all groups.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Results (Page 21, line 403-409).
13. The authors may opine about the fate of modified MSCs if kept in culture, and the
liposomal load if they passage or divide, and what could be the shelf life of this modified
MSC construct. Additionally, the authors may evaluate whether liposome internalization is
affecting surface labelling?
Response:
Thank you for your question. CD4 antibody-conjugated mBMSCs and the full AcM-DSS
system retained normal osteogenic, chondrogenic, and adipogenic differentiation (Fig 3g-i).
Due to chemical conjugation and intracellular small-molecule loading, the system is
unsuitable for extended passaging. Surface-conjugated antibodies remain stable after
cryopreservation, but small-molecule payloads may partially release after ~24 h; thus, loaded
compounds should be freshly prepared.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Discussion (Page 27, line 572-
576).
14. Since the MSCs are heavily modified and being proposed as a drug carrier, the authors
may be very precise and exact about the reproducibility of the protocols, with respect to
number of receptors and liposomes loaded.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. In the revised manuscript, we have provided
detailed quantitative descriptions of all procedures involved in the construction of the
AcM-DDS system in the Methods section, including receptor conjugation and liposome
loading steps. Each protocol has been independently repeated multiple times to ensure high
reproducibility and consistency of results.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Methods (Page 29, line 630-
640).
15. The authors mention in Line 407-409 that “However, such approaches, coupled with the
challenges of MSC production standardization, elevate treatment costs and increase clinical
complexity”. However, they may elaborate on how such heavy modifications of MSCs will
not increase the cost of production and therapy.
Response:
Thank you for your valuable question. We acknowledge that the AcM-DDS platform involves
additional processing steps compared with conventional BMSC therapy. The conjugation of
antibodies to MSCs is technically straightforward, and the main added cost arises from the
antibody itself. Likewise, the incorporation of small-molecule payloads primarily contributes
to the expense of the active compound rather than the cell-handling process. In current
BMSC-based therapies, such as Ryoncil (remestemcel-L), the major cost lies in cell
production—approximately USD 194,000 per intravenous infusion in the U.S. Notably, in our
PO model, the number of BMSCs that accumulated at inflammatory sites was about six times
higher for AcM-DDS than for unmodified BMSCs. Therefore, equivalent or superior
therapeutic efficacy could be achieved with one-sixth the number of BMSCs, suggesting that
the overall treatment cost of AcM-DDS, even after accounting for the antibody and small-
molecule components, would remain substantially lower than that of conventional BMSC
therapy.
16. The author may reference that CD-4 antibodies do not raise any safety concerns, as
mentioned in Line 423-428.
Response:
Thank you for the suggestion. As CD4 antibody Ibalizumab has been approved by the FDA,
indicating a favorable safety profile. We have added a reference in Line 133-134 of the
revised manuscript.
17. The authors may elaborate more about the limitations of the study.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion. Limitations of this study include the use
of murine MSCs and disease models that may not fully capture the complexity of human
immune responses. In future studies, antibodies with higher cellular specificity could be
selected to direct payloads toward more defined immune subsets, such as Th17, Th1, or Th2
cells, thereby enhancing targeting precision. In addition, all manufacturing steps were
conducted at the laboratory scale, and the scalability of the current AcM-DDS preparation
process to pilot or GMP-level production remains to be validated.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised discussion (Page 27, line 575-
581).
18. In line 474-375, the authors suggest that their system shows a broad translational potential
for immune disorders, however as also demonstrated in their own study, it seems that the
applicability of this system primarily depends on the pathophysiology of the disease.
Response:
Thanks for your careful review. The AcM-DDS platform offers broad translational potential
through two distinct avenues. First, antibody-conjugated BMSC therapy alone represents a
technically feasible and clinically relevant approach for autoimmune diseases. Similar
antibody-conjugated immune cell therapies—such as antibody-tagged NK cells and γδT
cells—are already in clinical development (Acea Therapeutics, clinical pipeline). If our
product progresses toward clinical translation, the use of a clinically approved CD4 antibody
(Ibalizumab, FDA-approved) provides an additional safety and regulatory advantage.
Therefore, from both a manufacturing and safety perspective, CD4mAb-BMSC–based
therapy has a realistic potential for clinical application. Of course, the pathological features of
diseased tissues can provide specific target receptors for selecting appropriate antibodies in
our delivery system. Therefore, elucidating the pathological characteristics of the lesion—
particularly the disease-specific receptors—is essential for the effective application of our
platform.
Second, the full AcM-DDS system, which combines antibody-conjugated BMSCs with drug-
loaded liposomes, requires freshly prepared and additional validation of payload safety. Since
Cedirogant has not yet completed all clinical evaluations, clinical translation of the AcM-DDS
system would likely involve substituting Cedirogant with an FDA-approved small-molecule
payload. These considerations together support the flexibility and adaptability of the AcM-
DDS platform for future therapeutic development.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised discussion (Page 27, line 564-
575).

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript presents a state-of-the-art drug delivery strategy that combines antibody-
conjugated mesenchymal stem cells with drug-loaded liposomes to achieve targeted drug
release at inflammatory sites. The therapeutic potential is evaluated in both acute (psoriasis)
and chronic (rheumatoid arthritis) mouse models of autoimmune diseases.
The Antibody-Conjugated MSCs Drug Delivery System (AcM-DDS) is highly innovative and
conjugates several therapeutic advantages specifically associated with the trophic and
immunomodulatory effects of BMSC (confirmed in the in vivo experiments by the
administration of BMSC alone) with the possibility to 1) conjugate antigen-specific
antibodies (in this case for the CD4 antigen expressed on T cells) onto the BMSC surface to
enhance their homing efficiency, 2) transform antibody-conjugated BMSCs (CD4-mBMSC)
into cargo cells (AcM-DDS ) for small-molecule drugs (in this study, Cdg, a RORγt inverse
agonist) enabling targeted delivery to sites of inflammation.
The study is well written and results are robust, built on carefully conducted and
technologically solid experiments supporting this novel strategy for drug delivery in the
treatment of autoimmune diseases. A few aspects of the study require clarification and
revision to strengthen the manuscript.
General comment:
Because AcM-DDS can target any membrane protein, enabling more flexible and precise drug
delivery, we wonder why authors used the broadly expressed CD4 antigen to target T cells,
involved in AID pathogenesis. Although the delivery of Cdg, a RORγt inverse agonist, mainly
restricts the drug effect on Th17 cells, the use of CD4 to guide AcM-DDS toward the sites of
inflammation in IMQ-induced PO mice and in the CIA mouse model of RA poses, in a larger
perspective, some concerns about the risk of targeting CD4+ T cells, a T cell subsets playing
major roles in physiological immune responses. While the lack of abnormalities, observed in
major organs (heart, liver, lungs and kidneys), may reflect the safety of AcM-DDS in these
mouse models, assessed in a pathogen free environment, a different outcome may be observed
upon an infectious trigger and in humans. Authors should comment on this issue in the
discussion.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate your recognition of our study and your thoughtful review. CD4 was
chosen as the targeting antigen during the proof-of-concept stage of the AcM-DDS platform.
The selection criteria included (i) high expression of CD4 in inflamed tissues enriched with
activated T cells, (ii) presence of CD4 on Th17 cells, which are the intended recipients of
Cedirogant delivery, and (iii) the availability of an FDA-approved CD4 antibody
(Ibalizumab), which provides a favorable safety precedent. Importantly, CD4 itself is not a
therapeutic target in this context but serves to direct BMSCs and their encapsulated small
molecules toward inflamed regions. The successful proof-of-concept using CD4 supports the
feasibility of AcM-DDS, and future iterations can employ disease-specific antigens (e.g., IL-
23R or CCR6) for enhanced targeting precision.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Results (Page 6, line 131-135).
Major points:
1. Why did authors change the administration protocol for the PO and RA mouse models
experiments (i.v. in the tail vein for the IMQ study vs retro-orbital venous injection for the
CIA mouse model)? Importantly, no data are provided to evaluate the biodistribution of MSCs
following retroorbital administration. Authors should assess whether this alternative route
leads to differences in organ accumulation
Response:
Thank you for your thoughtful question. We chose retro-orbital venous injection for the CIA
mouse model due to significant challenges with tail vein injection in this model. Specifically,
collagen and Freund’s adjuvant emulsions are injected subcutaneously near the tail base twice
during the model setup, which always leads to severe local inflammation, causing persistent
lesions or even tail loss in some cases. This made tail vein injection unfeasible.
Given this issue, we opted for retro-orbital venous injection, which has turned out to be
technically easier to perform. In our preliminary experiments, we used IVIS imaging to assess
the biodistribution of DiD-labeled mBMSCs and CD4-mBMSCs. The results showed that
CD4-mBMSCs preferentially accumulated in the limbs and at the tail base, where the
inflammation from the CIA model was most pronounced. We have included these data in
Supplementary Fig. 12 to clarify any concerns about biodistribution. We hope this explanation
addresses your concern and clarifies the rationale for our approach.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Results (Page 19, line 374-377).
2. In general, authors use citations quite unscrupulously particularly in the introduction
section. A few examples: In lines 30-32, the statement “Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have
shown promising potential in the treatment of autoimmune diseases (AIDs) such as psoriasis
(PO)1, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)2, multiple sclerosis (MS)3, inflammatory bowel
disease (IBD)4, and rheumatoid arthritis (RA)5” is not directly supported by the references.
Ref 6 (Pittenger et al, 1999) does not cover the anti-inflammatory properties of MSC. Ref 8
refers to MSC and B cells (and not Tregs) and Ref 9 uses a mice model defective of Tregs and
therefore is not appropriate to support the effect of MSC on Tregs. More references are not
totally appropriate along the text. Overall, authors are invited to carefully go through the text
to ensure that citations properly support what they are claiming.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out this important issue. We apologize for the
inappropriate or imprecise use of some references in the initial submission. In the revised
manuscript, we have thoroughly re-examined and carefully cross-checked all citations
throughout the text to ensure that each reference accurately supports the corresponding
statement.
Minor comments
1. Authors use the term “Mesenchymal Stem Cells”, rather than “Mesenchymal Stromal
Cells” which is now preferred. As the manuscript does not address any issue related to their
regenerative potential and they only demonstrated that modified BMSC can differentiate into
the osteogenic lineage, we would suggest using the term “Mesenchymal Stromal Cells” in the
title and along the whole manuscript.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive suggestion. We fully agree
with the point raised regarding terminology. Indeed, “Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (MSCs)” is
the currently preferred nomenclature, particularly in contexts where regenerative potential is
not the primary focus. In light of this valuable feedback, we have carefully revised the
manuscript, including the title and all relevant sections, to consistently use “Mesenchymal
Stromal Cells” throughout. We greatly appreciate your guidance in helping us improve the
clarity and accuracy of our manuscript.
2. In the legend for Figure 1, the authors should include a brief description of the design
framework and experimental workflow.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate this insightful suggestion. We have revised the Figure 1 legend to
include a concise overview of the study design and experimental workflow. In addition, we
added panels d–e to depict the therapeutic application of CD4mAb-conjugated BMSCs loaded
with RORγt inverse agonists in the IMQ-induced PO and CIA models. We believe these
updates enhance the clarity and informativeness of Figure 1.
3. In lines 141-143, the authors claim “CD4-mBMSCs exhibited significantly enhanced
binding to multiple CD4⁺ T cells, confirming their targeted binding capacity toward CD4⁺ T
cells at inflammatory sites”. These data refer to confocal imaging, and quantitative analyses
are needed to support the data.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point, which was also noted by
another reviewer. We acknowledge that the original manuscript did not present explicit
quantification of CD4⁺ T cell binding to CD4-mBMSCs, and we apologize for this oversight.
In response, we have now performed quantification of the binding shown in the original Fig.
2d (now Fig. 2e). Specifically, N₃-mBMSCs and CD4-mBMSCs were co-cultured with CD4⁺
T cells, and the ratio of CD4⁺ T cells bound per MSC was calculated across 10 randomly
selected fields from three independent experiments (NEW Fig. 2f). Repeated experiments
yielded consistent results, confirming that the duration of co-culture did not influence
binding. Furthermore, by examining different T cell-to-MSC ratios, we observed that higher T
cell numbers led to increased binding to CD4-mBMSCs (NEW Supplementary Fig. 2b-c).
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Results (Page 7, line 148-159).
4. Why distribution of CD4-mBMSC did drop at 72 hours following i.v. administration
(compared to high levels at 24 and 96h)?
Response:
Thank you for this question, but in our experiments, we did not observe a decrease in
CD4‑mBMSC distribution at 72 h (Fig. 2g). We apologize if our phrasing led to any
misunderstanding.
5. Although the manuscript describes the preparation of the AcM-DDS system, it does not
provide quantitative data on the percentage of cells successfully conjugated or loaded.
Response:
We sincerely thank you for raising this insightful and important point regarding the
quantitative characterization of our system. A similar concern was also raised by another
reviewer, and we have taken it very seriously. In the revised manuscript, we now provide
detailed quantification of antibody conjugation: when 25 µg of DBCO-CD4mAb-FITC was
incubated with 1 × 10⁶ N₃-mBMSCs, approximately 2,500 antibody molecules were anchored
per cell on average (Page 6, Line 144-146).
In addition, while addressing this request, we also performed quantitative analysis of
nanoparticle uptake. Based on Cy5 fluorescence intensity, each CD4-mBMSC internalized
approximately 1.15 × 10⁴ CdgLipo particles per cell on average (Page 9, Line 201-204). The
experimental procedures for these quantifications have been detailed in the Methods section
for clarity and reproducibility.
6. In Figure 5d/e and Supplementary Figure 7, the authors present heat maps and cytokine
quantifications to support the anti-inflammatory effect of AcM-DDS. In lines 277–279, they
claim that “Importantly, AcM-DDS treatment led to a substantial downregulation of these
cytokines, suggesting a potent anti-inflammatory effect mediated by suppression of Th17-
driven immune responses”. However, based on the quantification of IL-17A, the reduction
appears comparable across the different treatment groups and does not clearly indicate a
distinct effect from AcM-DDS. Authors should comment in the text.
Response:
We sincerely thank you for this important comment and apologize for the previous wording,
which was not sufficiently precise. We have now revised the manuscript to clarify that,
according to the Luminex results, the reduction of IL-17A in the mBMSCs, CD4-mBMSCs,
CdgLipo, and AcM-DDS groups was generally comparable. Nevertheless,
immunofluorescence analysis of local dorsal skin tissue indicated that AcM-DDS produced a
more pronounced suppression of Th17-related cytokines such as IL17A, IL-21 and IL-22,
suggesting that its superior anti-inflammatory effect is primarily exerted at the local tissue
level.
“Treatment with AcM-DDS, as well as mBMSCs, CD4-mBMSCs, and CdgLipo, led to an
overall downward trend in these cytokines, indicating effective attenuation of
inflammation. Notably, although reductions in IL-17A and GM-CSF were comparable
among the cell-based and liposomal treatments (Fig. 5f-g), immunofluorescence analysis
revealed a more pronounced local suppression of IL17A, IL-21 and IL-22 by AcM-DDS,
suggesting that its superior modulation may primarily occur at the tissue
microenvironment level rather than in total tissue cytokine content.” (Page 6, Line 325-
331)
7. Why was IL-17A and RORγt expression only partially reduced in the CD4-mBMSCs mice
group, considering that in the Luminex Multiplex Assay the effect on inflammatory cytokines
was quite significant (Fig 5)?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The apparent discrepancy reflects
differences in assay scope and tissue kinetics. The Luminex assay analyzes whole‑skin lysates
and integrates signals from multiple cellular sources, hence the pronounced global decrease in
inflammatory cytokines with CD4‑mBMSCs. By contrast, immunofluorescence captures a
localized, section‑level snapshot. At this compartment, IL‑17A/RORγt can be partially
sustained by non‑CD4 sources (e.g., dermal γδ T cells, ILC3s) and residual upstream
IL‑23/IL‑1β–chemokine signaling, with additional temporal lag between upstream
suppression and terminal epidermal readouts. Consequently, IL‑17A/RORγt appear only
partially reduced by IF at the sampling time point, while whole‑tissue Luminex reveals a
robust overall anti‑inflammatory effect. These readouts are complementary rather than
contradictory.
We have also incorporated this explanation into the revised Results (Page 17, line 334-338).
8. In lines 131 and 140, the fluorophores FAM and DiI are mentioned. These should be
identified as fluorescent dyes when first introduced.
Response:
Thank you for the careful review and helpful suggestion. We agree and have revised the
manuscript to explicitly identify FAM and DiI as fluorescent dyes at their first mention. We
have also applied this convention consistently to any other fluorescent dyes upon first
introduction throughout the text.
9. In lines 142-143, the authors state that “confirming their targeted binding capacity toward
CD4⁺ T cells at inflammatory sites”. However, the data comes from in vitro co-culture
experiments. Therefore, the statement “at inflammatory sites” is misleading.
Response:
We sincerely thank you for this careful and insightful comment. We fully agree that the phrase
“at inflammatory sites” could be misleading, as the current data are derived from in vitro co-
culture experiments rather than in vivo inflammatory models. Accordingly, we have revised
the sentence to read:
“Confocal imaging revealed that, compared to N₃-mBMSCs, CD4-mBMSCs exhibited
significantly enhanced binding to multiple CD4⁺ T cells, confirming their targeted binding
capacity toward CD4⁺ T cells in vitro.” (Page 7, line 151-153)
10. In the legend of Figure 2e, the authors should add the imaging technique used to acquire
the data.
Response:
Thank you for your careful review and suggestion. We have revised the original legend of Fig
2e (now Fig 2g) to explicitly state the imaging technique.
“g, In vivo fluorescence imaging acquired using an IVIS imaging system of DiD-stained
mBMSCs or CD4-mBMSCs in IMQ-induced PO mice at 24 h, 72 h, and 96 h after
intravenous injection.”
11. The sections describing the generation of CD4-antibody-conjugated MSCs lack clarity,
and the methodology is difficult to follow. The authors should improve the readability of the
text.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We apologize for the lack of clarity in the
original description. In the revised manuscript, we have substantially revised and expanded
this section to provide a clearer, step-by-step description of the process, including detailed
information on reagent concentrations, reaction conditions, incubation times, and purification
steps.
We have also incorporated this modification into the revised Methods (Page 29, line 630-
640).
12. For the supplementary movies, the authors should add a figure legend.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. Legends have been added to the supplementary
movies as follows:
“Supplementary Movie a: Real‑time confocal imaging of mBMSCs taking up
Cy5‑CdgLipo in situ.
Supplementary Movie b: Real‑time confocal imaging of mBMSCs taking up free Cy5 in
situ.”

Comment:
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed
